blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: The Gaussian Mumford-Shah model segments an image into regions by minimizing a continuous multivariate Gaussian negative log-likelihood term plus a perimeter penalty. It is used for scalar- and vector-valued images, in particular hyperspectral images, but the existence of a minimizer in general is not guaranteed. The energy is unbounded below whenever the covariance of a single region degenerates, regardless of the perimeter of the regions. A quantitative covariance floor on the covariances of all regions, or equivalently uniform Hölder continuity with exponent at most one of all one-dimensional marginals of the histogram, guarantees a lower bound on the energy and the existence of a minimizer. Our approach therefore shows that existence follows from a property of the histogram of the image, and we furthermore argue that scale-independent covariance floors cannot exist. Admitting a quantitative covariance floor is generic: it holds almost surely for all images with suitable noise. As applications of our theory, we show the convergence of regularized models used in practice and of numerical methods.

blocks.en:
This paper starts by discussing the theoretical aspects of the CFC. In particular, we show that satisfying the CFC is equivalent to the marginal distributions of g g being Hölder continuous uniformly in y ∈ S N − 1 y\in S^{N-1} and that p ≥ 2 p\geq 2 is necessary.
It is then argued that the pushforward measure of g g , the continuous version of the histogram, is the correct invariant for the existence of covariance floors. Using techniques from Fourier analysis, we prove that a noisy image will almost surely satisfy the CFC. This section is independent of the Gaussian Mumford–Shah context. In the following section, we use information theory to show that the GMS admits a lower bound for images satisfying the CFC. With this lower bound at hand, we turn to our applications, which cover the existence of minimizers of the GMS and the convergence of the alternating minimization. The final section contains some numerical experiments illustrating our main theorems.
